newsitem.title: USA: U.S. farm co-ops aim to resurrect vetoed tax break.
newsitem.headline: U.S. farm co-ops aim to resurrect vetoed tax break.

text.p: U.S. farm cooperatives said they hoped to resurrect a tax break that fell victim Monday to the first use of a presidential line-item veto and, some say, misinformation.
"We're just reviewing all the options that are available to us," said Randy Jones, senior vice-president of the National Council of Farmer Cooperatives. "We're deeply disappointed."

President Clinton used the line-item veto to strike down a provision that would have allowed food processors to defer paying capital gains taxes on the sale of assets to qualified farmer cooperatives.
A similar tax break exists now for companies that sell stock to an employee stock ownership plan (ESOP).
Clinton also cancelled two other provisions of the balanced budget accord he signed into law last week. The cost of the food tax break was estimated at $98 million over five years.

Most of the attention surrounding the food processors tax break has focused on a supposed benefit for Harold Simmons, a Texas multimillionaire and Republican campaign contributor, who recently transferred control of some of his assets to a sugar cooperative.
Simmons denied in a statement he would have received any additional tax benefit from the provision.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told reporters the White House focused on farmer co-ops -- and not on the Simmons case -- when it reviewed the food processors provisions.
The president expressed sympathy for the goal of the food tax break, which was to make it easier for farmer cooperatives to buy processing facilities, but said it was poorly designed.

"This provision would have allowed a very limited number of agri-businessess to avoid paying capital gains taxes, possibly forever," on asset sales to farmer's cooperatives, he said. "It could have benefited not only traditional farm coops, but giant cooperations which do not need and should not trigger the benefits."
Clinton promised to work with Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota to recast the provision.
The farm co-op group said the veto was an "unfair and unjustified" act that excluded cooperatives from getting the same tax break as other employee-owned organisations.
Simmons controls Valhi Inc, which this year formed a "limited liability company" with the Snake River Sugar Co., a farmer co-op with about 2,000 members in the Northwest.

That transaction transferred control of four sugar beet processing plants to the cooperative, but not the title, said John Lemke, counsel for the Amalgamated Sugar Co., the firm formed by the deal. Amalgamated has its headquarters in Utah.
"Our deal is done," Lemke told Reuters in a telephone interview, disputing government estimates that the vetoed tax provision would have led to a huge new tax break for Simmons.

The transaction was completed in January and structured under current law in a way that "did not result in a taxable event for Simmons," Lemke said. Opponents of the provision must have "looked up their old notes and forgot that the transaction had been done," he said.
The vetoed provision would have allowed the Snake River coop to restruture its deal with Valhi, but even that would not have generated any more tax breaks for Simmons, Lemke said.
Instead, it would just give "outright ownership of the sugar assets" to cooperatives, with "no additional money changing hands," he said.
House Agriculture Committee Chairman Bob Smith, an Oregon Republican, also expressed disappointment with Clinton's veto, saying it hurt family farms which depend on some 4,000 regional cooperatives.
Representative Kenny Hulshof, a Missouri Republican who played a key role in getting the measure in the tax bill, angrily denounced Clinton's action.

"It is unfortunate at a time when America's farmers are battling the weather and battling the markets, they must battle their president," Hulshof said. By encouraging farmers to get into food processing, the tax break would have left them better prepared for the new era of reduced government support, he said.
